strengths: Framing visual attribution as a differentiable permutation learning task to directly optimize Deletion and Insertion metrics via Gumbel-Sinkhorn sorting relaxation is a highly original and theoretically sound contribution.

The proposed amortized framework achieves a remarkable trade-off between attribution quality and speed, enabling single-forward-pass inference (0.016s) with an optional test-time refinement that is still orders of magnitude faster than existing metric-driven optimization methods like MDA.

Excellent and comprehensive quantitative evaluation on ImageNet across diverse architectures (ViT-B/16, ViT-B/32, ConvNeXt Small), demonstrating state-of-the-art performance across multiple faithfulness metrics.
The qualitative results are exceptionally sharp, dense, and boundary-aligned, drastically improving upon the coarse, blocky, patch-level attributions typical of other vision transformer explainers.

Thoughtful training strategies (such as region-based permutation, grid augmentation, and sampling) effectively address the practical challenges of training high-resolution differentiably-sorted models, and the shortcut-detection experiment successfully proves the utility of test-time refinement for OOD scenarios.
weaknesses: The method is model-specific, meaning a separate explainer must be trained from scratch for each target model, which requires access to a representative training dataset and introduces offline training overhead.
The explainer architecture is heavy, relying on a large frozen backbone (DINOv3 ViT-L/16), which may restrict its applicability on resource-constrained hardware despite the fast inference speed.

strengths: Direct Optimization of Metrics: The formulation of directly training an explainer by optimizing the non-differentiable Deletion and Insertion metrics using a Gumbel-Sinkhorn continuous relaxation is technically sound, elegant, and highly intuitive.

Fast Amortized Inference: Once trained, the explainer produces high-quality, pixel-level attributions in a single forward pass (at $T=0$), effectively bypassing the prohibitive computational cost associated with per-sample perturbation-based optimization methods like MDA.

Excellent Spatial Resolution: Unlike most ViT-specific visual attribution approaches that operate strictly at the patch level (resulting in blocky maps), AHA produces detailed, boundary-aligned, and dense pixel-level explanations.

Extensive Evaluation: The authors evaluate their method comprehensively across multiple classifiers (ViT-B/16, ViT-B/32, and ConvNeXt Small) and metrics (Deletion, Insertion, Positive, Negative, ADP, PIC) using different reference image modes, showing robust quantitative and qualitative gains.

Test-Time Refinement & Shortcut Detection: The optional few-step test-time refinement provides a flexible computational trade-off and shows great promise in out-of-distribution scenarios, such as successfully identifying injected shortcut artifacts.
weaknesses: Heavy Explainer Architecture: The explainer model relies on a frozen DINOv3 ViT-L/16 backbone combined with a DPT-inspired decoder. While the runtime during inference is very fast, the parameter footprint and memory usage of the explainer itself are extremely large compared to standard post-hoc approaches, which may limit deployment in resource-constrained environments.

Target Model Specificity: The explainer needs to be retrained for each target model to be explained. Although this is typical for amortized explainers, it limits immediate plug-and-play usability on arbitrary classifiers compared to propagation or pure post-hoc perturbation methods.

Hyperparameter Sensitivity Analysis: The framework relies on several sensitive parameters, such as the Gumbel-Sinkhorn temperature ($\tau$), the number of Sinkhorn iterations, grid sizes ($G$), and multiple loss weights ($\lambda_{\text{del}}, \lambda_{\text{ins}}, \lambda_{\text{reg}}$). A more detailed ablation or discussion on the sensitivity of these hyperparameters would further strengthen the paper.

strengths: Direct optimization of Deletion and Insertion metrics via a Gumbel-Sinkhorn differentiable sorting relaxation is a highly logical, technically sound, and elegant solution to the non-differentiability of ranking-based evaluation metrics.

Smart engineering designs, such as region-based permutations, perturbation step sampling, and grid augmentations, are introduced to make the training of the amortized explainer computationally tractable and robust to high-frequency artifacts.

The hybrid approach is highly versatile. It provides a fast, zero-shot single forward pass (T=0) that already achieves strong performance, alongside a cheap test-time refinement option (T>0) that allows for sample-specific adjustments and trade-offs between computation and attribution quality.

Comprehensive evaluation across multiple architectures (ViT-B/16, ViT-B/32, ConvNeXt-S) and a wide suite of metrics. The results consistently demonstrate state-of-the-art or highly competitive performance in terms of both faithfulness and runtime.

The shortcut-learning detection experiment in Appendix A.3 is exceptional; it clearly demonstrates how the test-time refinement allows the explainer to identify model-specific artifacts (like the white circle) even when the base explainer was trained on clean data.
weaknesses: The explainer model uses a powerful pre-trained DINOv3 ViT-L/16 backbone and a DPT decoder. Because of the strong semantic and segment-like representation inherent to DINOv3, there is a risk that the produced attribution maps look visually appealing and boundary-aligned primarily due to the backbone's priors, rather than the target model's actual decision process.

To rule out the concern of semantic priors dominating the attribution, the paper lacks a rigorous sanity check as proposed by Adebayo et al. (e.g., cascading parameter randomization of the target classifier). It is important to demonstrate that the amortized explainer's output significantly degrades or completely changes when the target classifier's weights are randomized, proving it is indeed faithful to the target model and not just acting as an object co-segmentation tool.

The approach requires retraining a separate explainer model for every new target model and dataset. This amortized training overhead limits immediate, out-of-the-box applicability compared to traditional gradient- or propagation-based methods.

The formulation relies on many hyperparameters (temperature $\tau$, weighting factors $\lambda_{del}, \lambda_{ins}, \lambda_{reg}$, number of steps $S$, grid sizes, etc.). An ablation study or sensitivity analysis of these parameters would help in understanding the robustness and ease of tuning of the training pipeline.
